anti_overlap: Does not cover real-world sociological coverage of vocational types or labor-history gaps — that is fd-labor-sociology-vocational.
Does not cover how vocation interacts with the game's six locked axes or cross-axis combinatorics — that is fd-life-sim-career-mechanics.
Does not cover vocational identity formation as a psychological process — that is fd-vocational-psychology-identity.
decision_lens: Would a TTRPG designer split this value into two background options, and if so, what is the mechanical and tonal difference between them — or is the coarsening justified by the game's procedural purpose?
focus: Vocational identity as mechanical anchor: how TTRPG background and origin systems enumerate vocation-as-character-substrate, where over-bundling destroys expressive resolution, and which clustering choices have proven load-bearing across D&D 5e, PF2e, Vampire: the Masquerade, and World of Darkness
name: fd-rpg-background-taxonomy
persona: Apply the perspective of a TTRPG character-background-system designer who has shipped or deeply analyzed systems in the D&D / Pathfinder / World of Darkness lineage — they care about whether each vocation value is a distinct identity anchor (not just a job description), measure success by whether two characters who share a vocation value are recognizably the same type of person while remaining individually distinct, and flag any value that is doing so much aggregation work that it collapses meaningfully different character types into a single undifferentiated bucket.
review_areas: D&D 5e's 'guild artisan' background was criticized for covering glassblowers, jewelers, potters, weaponsmiths, and leatherworkers under one identity anchor — PF2e's later split distinguished craft-guild (object-focused, transaction-oriented) from artisan-guild (skill-prestige, apprenticeship-coded) because the metis signatures are different. Apply this lens to `trades-skilled`: carpenter, machinist, and mechanic have distinct tool relationships, problem-solving registers, and body-types. Assess whether the value needs a sub-typology or whether the axis's cross-product with class-coding and region-coding does enough disambiguation.

`caregiver` is the most over-bundled value in the proposed taxonomy: K-12 teacher, nurse, hospice worker, EMT, priest, librarian, and social worker all occupy this bucket. In WoD/VtM terms, these are different 'concepts' even if they share the service-orientation trait. Evaluate each against the metis-bearer criterion (§2.10): a hospice nurse's metis is time/body/death; a parish priest's metis is ritual/community/listening; a K-12 teacher's metis is attention/developmental-pattern/institutional-survival. These are not the same type of guy. Assess the cost of bundling versus the combinatorial explosion of splitting.

The Pathfinder 2e 'background as identity-plus-skill-anchor' model suggests that each background should produce a character with a recognizable set of world-relationships, not just job history. Evaluate each of the 13 vocation values through this lens: does `commerce-large` produce a recognizable set of world-relationships (deference to hierarchy, legibility of spreadsheets, comfort with abstraction), or is it a catch-all for 'office guy' that lacks the specificity required for procedural characterization?

World of Darkness clan/concept design principle: the most successful WoD archetypes are vocational types that have a distinctive relationship to power, information, and embodiment simultaneously — not just job categories. The Tremere (scholar-mage) and Nosferatu (surveillance-network) are vocation-as-information-access. Assess whether the 13 values carry this triple signature, or whether some (e.g., `tech-work`) are defined by a single dimension (technical skill) without the characteristic relationship to power or embodiment that makes them generative character anchors.

The `creative-credentialed` vs `creative-freelance` split mirrors PF2e's scholar vs street-performer distinction — the former is institutionally legible, the latter depends on reputation networks. Assess whether this is the right fault line for the game's purposes, or whether the more characterologically load-bearing distinction is creative-as-identity vs creative-as-career (i.e., does the person define themselves by the work, or by the credentials?). The journalist who lost their industry may now be creative-freelance but was formed by creative-credentialed — is the trajectory mismatch captured by the two-field design, or does it need a value of its own?

Evaluate whether `military` is doing appropriate work as a single value or whether the career-military vs formative-only distinction (already noted in the brief) is doing too much work for the label. In TTRPG terms, 'soldier' backgrounds typically distinguish enlisted vs officer vs intelligence vs special operations because the metis signatures differ radically — discipline-and-hierarchy is the military's unifying metis, but the specific form (physical endurance vs institutional navigation vs tradecraft) varies. Assess whether the vocation_formative × vocation_current trajectory design adequately handles this or whether a sub-type modifier is needed.

severity_examples.condition: If priest, hospice nurse, K-12 teacher, EMT, and librarian all roll `caregiver` as their vocation, the downstream characterization system must produce recognizably different Uncs from the same value — and if it cannot (because the characterization is handled at the vocation level, not at a sub-type level), the game generates five characters who are tonally indistinguishable despite having radically different metis signatures, embodiments, and network-relationships.
severity_examples.scenario: `caregiver` collapses five distinct Unc-types into one identity bucket

severity_examples.condition: If the downstream generator treats all `trades-skilled` Uncs as sharing the same posture, vocabulary, and world-relationship, the value is doing too much aggregation work — a machinist's relationship to tolerance, material behavior, and industrial-facility geography differs from a carpenter's relationship to wood-grain, site conditions, and client relationships. The TTRPG precedent (guild artisan splitting) suggests this bundling has costs that increase as the characterization system becomes more expressive.
severity_examples.scenario: `trades-skilled` lacks the metis-differentiation to distinguish carpenter from machinist from mechanic

severity_examples.condition: If `commerce-large` generates characters whose distinguishing features are primarily class-coding (professional, finance-money) rather than vocation-specific metis, the value is redundant with the class-coding axis rather than additive. The question is whether there is a recognizable `commerce-large` Unc who could not be produced by combining a different vocation with the same class value.
severity_examples.scenario: `commerce-large` produces a 'generic office guy' with no distinctive metis signature

success_hints: The PF2e split-test: for any value that feels over-bundled, ask 'would a TTRPG background-system designer publish these as two separate backgrounds with distinct mechanical and tonal hooks?' If yes, assess the cost of splitting vs. the cost of coarsening.

Each value should pass the 'distinctive world-relationship' test: does this vocation produce a character with a recognizable relationship to power, information, and embodiment simultaneously — or only to one of the three?

The WoD concept-vs-clan distinction: vocation value is the identity anchor (clan), but the specific form of vocation practice is the character concept. Assess whether the 13 values are operating at the clan level (broad enough to encompass variation) or have been pushed to the concept level (too specific to be generative).
task_context: Reviewing the 13 proposed vocation-coding axis values for Unc Rancher's procedural character generation system through the lens of TTRPG background-system design — assessing over-bundling, under-splitting, and whether each value functions as a load-bearing identity anchor rather than a job category.
